key_expressions: We should clarify the initial direction,
I'm unsure where to set the project scope,
I’m a bit concerned about potential risks,
Do you have any other thoughts,

A: I'm still unsure how to define the starting point of this project. What do you think?
The overall direction feels a bit vague, which is worrying me.
You're right — I should set the foundation more firmly before moving forward.
B: I felt the same! Once the starting point is clear, the whole structure becomes steadier.
Exactly — if the direction is fuzzy early on, the middle phases tend to wobble.
Good call. That approach will make the entire workflow much more coherent.

A: I'm struggling to decide how wide the project scope should be.
If we make it too broad, the schedule could get overwhelming.
Alright, I’ll group only the core features and begin from there.
B: Scope-setting is always tricky — if it’s off, resources drain fast!
Right, and the schedule tightens until there’s no buffer left.
Focusing on the essentials first will definitely stabilize the workflow.

A: I think we need to adjust the project priorities. What do you think?
At this pace, the critical phases might get pushed back.
Let me reorganize the priority list from the top.
B: Great idea — updating priorities alone makes everything clearer.
Exactly, delaying critical phases can disrupt the entire timeline.
Once you reorganize them, the next steps will become much easier.

A: I think we should do a risk assessment earlier than planned.
I can’t quite pinpoint where the biggest issues might arise.
I'll start by reviewing the parts with the highest dependency.
B: Yes, the earlier we identify risks, the easier they are to manage.
Dependency-heavy areas always bring the most uncertainty.
Once you check those, the overall risk map will become much clearer.

A: The timeline is more complicated than I expected.
I'm unsure where to place the mid-project review.
I’ll reset the review points based on the key milestones.
B: Absolutely — a clear timeline already solves half the project!
Once the review point is fixed, adjustments become much easier.
Using milestones as anchors will make the whole plan predictable.

A: While organizing the meeting notes, I noticed some interpretation gaps.
It seems people understood certain terms differently.
I’ll standardize the terminology first so we avoid confusion.
B: Exactly — consistent terminology prevents so many misunderstandings.
Especially during planning, even small wording differences can cause major issues.
Once terminology is aligned, documentation will flow much more smoothly.

A: I’d like to clarify the role division among team members.
When responsibilities overlap, things get messy quickly.
So I’ll update the role definition table to make everything clearer.
B: Absolutely — overlapping duties always lead to duplicated work.
Clear responsibility boundaries speed up every stage.
Once you update it, collaboration will feel much more organized.

A: I heard the external partner’s schedule might be unstable.
I’m worried this could delay our entire timeline.
I’ll prepare a contingency plan before things escalate.
B: I heard that too — external schedules tend to have many variables.
Exactly, even one delay there can derail the whole plan.
A contingency plan will save us from unexpected setbacks.

A: Budget allocation is always the hardest part. It feels tight again.
It's tricky deciding what we should cut back.
I'll start by reviewing the fixed costs before adjusting anything else.
B: Budget issues never get easier… trimming it is always stressful!
Right — cutting too much can affect essential components.
Reviewing fixed costs first will give you a clearer overall picture.

A: I think the overall structure is nearly complete now.
I just want to review the flow once more.
I’ll wrap up the draft today using the feedback you shared.
B: It’s coming together really well — the whole plan feels solid.
A final flow check should bring everything to perfection.
Great, once you finalize it, the entire proposal will be much stronger!
